section_summary: This section continues a State Department memorandum prepared for 1933 conversations with a Japanese delegation before the Monetary and Economic Conference. It reviews economic disputes, Manchuria, American–Japanese relations, and likely Japanese positions, then supplies a Tokyo telegram, an economic review, and three press clippings as annexes. The section ends with records of conversations on May 25 and 26 about exchange stabilization, credit, silver, tariffs, and trade agreements; the May 26 record continues beyond page 227.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japan and preliminary conversations before the Monetary and Economic Conference
subfiles.about: Briefing on American–Japanese disputes and likely Japanese positions in forthcoming economic conversations.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews disputes over immigration, fisheries, mandated islands, and oil, then assesses tensions arising from Japan’s actions in Manchuria. It anticipates Japanese positions on exchange rates, tariffs, recognition, and the Open Door, while urging caution in conversations with Viscount Ishii. Its closing pages list five annexes.

subfiles.title: Annex I: Paraphrase of Ambassador Grew’s telegram on Japan’s conference policy
subfiles.about: Reports expected Japanese positions in the Washington conversations and London conference.
subfiles.summary: The embassy expects the delegation to seek approval from Tokyo before making commitments. It outlines likely positions on Asian affairs, disarmament, currency, credit, silver, trade restrictions, and tariffs.

subfiles.title: Annex II: Brief Economic Review of Japan With Particular Reference to Foreign Trade and the Part Played Therein by the United States
subfiles.about: Compiles statistics on Japanese trade, finance, and American investment.
subfiles.summary: The review compares Japan’s imports and exports in 1930–1932, including trade by partner and commodity, and discusses the effects of yen depreciation on an industrial recovery. It also tabulates national debt, gold reserves, budgets, American investments, and invisible trade.

subfiles.title: Annex III: People and Politics
subfiles.about: Profiles Viscount Ishii as Japan’s representative at the economic conferences.
subfiles.summary: Tucker describes Ishii’s diplomatic career, the difficulty of representing Japan after its withdrawal from the League of Nations, and Japan’s dependence on American trade.

subfiles.title: Annex IV: ‘Asia for Asiatics,’ Is the Japanese Policy
subfiles.about: Reports Ishii’s remarks in Honolulu about Japan’s Asian policy and the prospect of war.
subfiles.summary: Ishii describes an ‘Asia for Asiatics’ policy and says war with the United States is unlikely.

subfiles.title: Annex V: Japan to Ask Credit to Keep Yen Stable
subfiles.from: Shumnasuke Oishi, New York Journal of Commerce
subfiles.about: Reports anticipated Japanese requests for American support for yen stabilization.
subfiles.summary: The article says Japanese delegates may seek credits for exchange stabilization while favoring a return to gold in principle. It also outlines proposed positions on trade barriers, rice imports, tariffs, prices, and capital movement.

subfiles.title: Monetary and Economic Conference — Conversations
subfiles.summary: Divider for the ensuing conversation records.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Japanese delegates, May 25, 1933
subfiles.about: Records American and Japanese discussion of monetary and economic proposals.
subfiles.summary: Japanese delegates say they wish to prevent further yen depreciation but cannot promise a fixed exchange rate or spend scarce gold reserves to defend one. Participants discuss credit policy, capital movement, reserve requirements, silver, public works, and trade barriers. The meeting adjourns until May 26.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Japanese delegates, May 26, 1933
subfiles.about: Records discussion of trade barriers, most-favored-nation treatment, and a tariff truce.
subfiles.summary: American representatives favor bilateral trade agreements under unconditional most-favored-nation treatment and discuss a tariff truce. Japanese delegates express broad agreement while asking about exceptions, imperial preferences, and the truce’s wording. The record continues beyond this section.
